claims.text: Machine-learning models can be trained on binary-alloy datasets using expandable features and applied to multielement high-entropy alloys.
Expandable features derived from binary-alloy data can represent relevant information for multielement-alloy crystal-structure prediction.
The expandable features capture both the underlying structural and chemical properties of high-entropy alloys.
Machine learning can identify relationships between expandable features and alloy structural phases.
Machine learning can identify relationships between binary-derived expandable features and melting properties of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach could improve the accuracy of high-entropy-alloy melting-temperature prediction.
The proposed approach could improve prediction of latent heat of fusion and solid-liquid interface energy.
The proposed approach could make melting-property prediction more computationally efficient.
The proposed melting-property predictions would be more accurate and computationally efficient than traditional methods such as CALPHAD.
CALPHAD represents a current baseline for predicting the stated melting properties.
The method should remain valid for multielement high-entropy alloys whose compositions are representable by the binary-alloy training data.
A diverse binary-alloy training set is a condition for the proposed approach.
Prediction accuracy may depend on the quality and diversity of the binary-alloy datasets.
Prediction accuracy may depend on the particular machine-learning model employed.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing the proposed model with CALPHAD on high-entropy alloys having measured melting temperature, latent heat of fusion, and solid-liquid interface energy.
Failure to achieve a significant improvement in both accuracy and computational efficiency over traditional methods would falsify the hypothesis.
